new_statements.quote: The accent is fairly mobile, and, as in many dialects, it does not observe the rule of LP of falling on the end of the word. The local Yazdi form of bazari has its own peculiarity, keeping the accent on the first, instead of the last syllable, which sounds rather odd; though the accent is never sharp. Gabri has the accent on the first syllable only in some verbal forms. The accent seems to consist neither in merely raising the voice, nor in merely prolonging it, but in doing both, in a varying degree, depending on intonation, and, perhaps, on the rate of speech.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ivanow gives no positional rule: word accent is 'fairly mobile' and does not follow the Literary Persian (LP) final-stress rule; only some verbal forms carry initial accent (the local Persian koine of Yazd, 'bazari', is noted as initial-accenting). Elsewhere in the same grammar the definite suffix -é attracts the accent (p. 60), the aorist prefix e- may be stressed for future emphasis without taking the main accent (p. 78), the Kermani durative prefix i- is stressed in the perfect (p. 83), and the 3sg copula suffix -uné is only semi-accented, the main accent staying on the host word (p. 85). The only other first-hand statement, Toosarvandani & Farudi 2003 p. 26 (Qasemabad, Yazd), says 'stress in Dari is always on the first syllable of a verb' and treats tonic pronouns as separate stress domains; it says nothing about nouns.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Ivanow p. 85: in the 3sg copula suffix -uné 'u is very short, and é is semi-accented (as the real accent rests on the word itself)'. No general secondary-stress statement.
new_statements.exceptions: Definite/correlative suffix -é/-á attracts the accent (pitrügé 'the boy', wazîré; p. 60); the adverbial preverb bar 'out' is 'emphatic, attracting the accent' (p. 70); imperative bi- in biure/biwre 'is sharply accented' (p. 83); 'occasional difference in the accent in the two sub-dialects' Yazdi vs Kermani (p. 54).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent in connected speech as heard by Ivanow (fast talkers, no measurements); accent described as a mixture of pitch raising and lengthening 'depending on intonation'. Sub-dialects: Yazdi Gabri (YG) and Kermani Gabri (KG). The 2003 Farudi/Toosarvandani remark concerns verbs and clitic-vs-word tests in the Qasemabad (Yazd) dialect.
new_statements.identity_note: pars1252 'Parsi-Dari' [prd] is a Glottolog Bookkeeping entry that duplicates Zoroastrian Dari [gbz] = zoro1242 ('Zoroastrian Yazdi'; also Behdini, Gabri, Gavruni). Any catalog entry should be filed under zoro1242 and pars1252 marked as its duplicate. Ivanow 1935 describes 'Gabri' with two sub-dialects, Yazdi (YG) and Kermani (KG), and notes occasional accent differences between them; Toosarvandani & Farudi 2003 describe the Qasemabad dialect of Yazd. The Judeo-Yazdi penultimate-stress statement (Gindin, EIr) belongs to a different language and must not be attached here.

new_statements.quote: The first allomorph of each pair forms its own stress domain and for this reason it is believed to be a word, e.g. /'om 'āděn/ 'give it to me!' (stress is always on the first syllable of the word). The second allomorph is a right-attaching clitic, e.g. /'m-āděn/ 'give it to me!' or /'m-e tā/ 'he gives it to me.' [...] The syllabic variant of the simple past ergative marker pronouns never receive word stress, however, and must therefore be analyzed as clitics that attach syntactically to the right, to the verb, but do not have a phonological host.

new_statements.relation_note: The language is not in the catalog; the only existing statement is Ivanow 1935 (p. 48), which says the accent is 'fairly mobile', does not follow the Persian final-stress rule, and that Gabri 'has the accent on the first syllable only in some verbal forms'. Farudi & Toosarvandani instead state that stress is always word-initial (Qasemabad village dialect). The two agree only on verbs taking initial stress; on general word stress they differ (mobile vs fixed: initial syllable), and the authors' own later Summary of Findings retreats to verbs only.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the first syllable of the word; the statement is made in passing, as the diagnostic behind a clitic-versus-word test for the pronoun sets, and every stressed example is a verb ('āděn 'give!', 'biyo 'come!', 'vot 'said') or a monosyllabic noun stem plus clitic ('svā-m 'my dog', 'del-om 'my stomach'). The report has no phonology or prosody section.
new_statements.exceptions: Clitic pronouns are outside word stress: the non-syllabic object-pronoun allomorph, the left-attaching prepositional-object clitic, the possessive clitics, and the simple-past and participle ergative-marker pronouns 'never receive word stress'. The same authors' fuller 2003 'Summary of Findings' (p. 26, already held by the project) narrows the parenthesis to 'stress in Dari is always on the first syllable of a verb'.
new_statements.identity_note: Farudi & Toosarvandani describe the Qasemabad (Qāsemābād) village variety of Yazdi Dari, one of some thirty Zoroastrian village dialects around Yazd; Ivanow 1935 describes Yazdi Gabri more broadly. pars1252 is a Glottolog bookkeeping entry that duplicates Zoroastrian Dari zoro1242 (Behdini/Gabri/Gavruni [gbz]).

readall_conflicts: Ivanow 1935 (Rivista degli Studi Orientali 16: 48; the existing statement) describes the Yazdi Gabri accent as fairly mobile, not observing Persian final stress, with first-syllable accent only in some verbal forms and an odd initial accent in the local Yazdi form of bazari. Farudi & Toosarvandani's 2003 Preliminary Report (Qasemabad dialect) states in a parenthesis that stress is always on the first syllable of the word, with examples that are all verbs or monosyllabic stems; their fuller 2003 Summary of Findings (p. 26) narrows the same claim to the first syllable of a verb. So the sources disagree on general word stress (mobile vs fixed: initial syllable), while all three agree that verbs carry initial stress. The preliminary web report is the weakest of the three (no phonology section, clitic-test context, later narrowed by its own authors), so its fixed: initial syllable statement should be recorded with that caveat rather than taken as the language's rule.
